text: Fifty years of a country's history, cut down to thirteen minutes, mostly out of film that other cameras had already made. Denis Sanders assembled it in the United States within a year of the events the title names, close enough that the outcome was still unsettled while the edit was being cut. That proximity does something to the material. Each splice has to claim that one thing followed from another, and in 1969 nobody could yet be certain what would follow. The images themselves were shot for other reasons, most of them intended to last a week. Reassembled at this compression, half a century of a nation arrives as a single argument delivered at speed. It took the Academy Award for documentary short subject.

A father goes looking for the man who killed his daughter, and the picture turns out to be more interested in the father. Roy Calnek made it in 1926, sixty-three silent minutes in which pursuit gives way to something nearer reform: the man who set out to settle a death starts wanting a different life instead. Melodrama of the period had a settled machinery for that change, with the barroom as the place where a family's money and a man's character go the same way, and the moral accounting done in faces rather than title cards. Calnek uses the machinery plainly and without irony, for viewers who did not need the cost of a saloon explained to them. The National Film Registry keeps it.

The fruit is paper and paste, painted by hand, and none of it will ever rot. Chick Strand spends twenty-two minutes in the small Mexican workshop where young women make it, filming the job the way it feels from inside: colour first, then hands, then music, then the talk. The talk is mostly about men, and it does not stop. There is a wrinkle in the arrangement worth noticing, since the boss is a gringo and the factory belongs to his Mexican wife, so authority in the room runs along two lines at once. What holds the thing together is rhythm rather than argument: repetition turning into movement, and the running commentary of people who work close enough together to say anything at all.

Everything the two adults might say to each other has to pass through a six-year-old. Ok Hee likes the new boarder, so she carries what her widowed mother will not put into words, and the courtship advances at the speed of a child's understanding of it. Shin Sang-ok keeps the story inside a house of women, where a man renting the spare room is an event the neighbours will have views about, and makes the drama out of what is withheld: a glance held a beat too long, an errand run twice. South Korea sent the film to the Academy Awards as its submission. A hundred and three minutes is a long stretch to sustain on things that cannot be said, and it holds because of Ok Hee, the only person in the house with no reason to be careful.

Two Union pickets and a Confederate agree, across a brook, to stop shooting at each other for an hour. They negotiate it themselves, which is the whole premise; the truce runs sixty minutes of story and the film runs twenty-three. Denis Sanders shot it in black and white as a student at UCLA, working from an 1897 story by Robert W. Chambers called Pickets, and the small scale is not a compromise, since three men and one stretch of water is the exact size of the situation. What the hour produces is a difficulty. Aiming at a man becomes harder after an hour of his conversation. In 1955 it took the Academy Award for two-reel short subject.

In 1913 a man stands in front of a camera and makes an argument in a language the printed page cannot hold. George Veditz, once president of the National Association of the Deaf, is defending the right of deaf people to sign rather than speak, and he does it in American Sign Language, with nothing cut in to translate him. The form is the position. Motion pictures were less than twenty years old, and here the technology is put to the one job print had never managed: keeping a gesture where it can be seen again. Fourteen minutes, one speaker, a case made at length. He is addressing people who will understand him without assistance, and leaving the rest of the room to manage as best it can.

The house sits on a chicken farm; the livelihood is right outside the window. A composer works at home, his wife runs the business that pays for the work, and a young woman is hired and moves in, which in this arrangement means she is inside the marriage from her first day. The catalogue files it as crime, drama and horror at once, and the three do not compete: the fear is domestic and economic, a matter of who sleeps in which room, who earns, who can be dismissed and who cannot. Kim Ki-young keeps almost everything indoors and lets the pressure rise on a household scale. No monster is required. A live-in worker and a couple whose home and income occupy the same few rooms will do.

The proposal is modest to the point of looking like nothing: some members of a white Lutheran congregation in Omaha should meet Lutherans from the north side of the same city. Persuading them is the entire film. The minister makes his case, and then makes it again, and fifty-eight minutes proves long enough to watch an institution work out what it believes as against what it says on Sunday. Barbara Connell's camera was there in 1966, which means the film also keeps the vocabulary of 1966 intact, including the word the congregation uses for the people under discussion. The minister is the one exposed by the process. The congregation he is trying to move is also the congregation that employs him, and everyone in the room can do that arithmetic.

The violin costs more than the household has, and the household finds the money anyway. That transaction, years of small economies converted into an instrument for one boy, is what Frank Borzage's 1920 picture runs on, and it opens an account that playing well will not close. Leon learns, Leon becomes very good, and then people outside the family begin making claims of their own on him. Seventy-one minutes, silent, from a period when a studio could count on the story of parents spending everything on a child's gift. Borzage keeps the ordinary arithmetic visible: what a lesson costs, what a room holds, who goes without so the practice can continue. The playing has to register without a note of sound, which the film manages by watching people listen.

The steps of the Lincoln Memorial were not built as a stage, and in 1939 they were used as one. Eight minutes of film record Marian Anderson singing there, and the entire ambition of the thing is to be present while it happens. Open-air sound was not a solved problem in that decade: a voice with no walls to help it, weather, distance, and equipment that had to be hauled into position and left where it stood. What survives is therefore two records at once, the performance and the effort of catching the performance. The camera has one subject and stays with it. Against that much marble, a figure singing alone is a question of scale as much as of sound, and eight minutes is as long as the occasion needs.

The distinction attached to this one is narrow, and it carries weight: the first screen Uncle Tom played by a Black actor. The phrasing implies what the adaptations before it had been doing. William Robert Daly made it in 1914, fifty-four minutes drawn from a novel the stage had been working over for decades before any camera got near it. Harriet Beecher Stowe's book was common property by then, printed, performed and argued over, and the picture arrives into that traffic carrying most of what it inherited. The alteration is confined to a single role. It is not a small one, since the part is the title and the title is the whole property. A first of this kind records two facts at once: that it happened, and how long it took.

A family goes to the New York World's Fair in 1939 and is introduced, in sequence, to the machines meant to run the rest of the century. That is the plot. The fifty-five minutes are arranged so that a robot and a dishwasher can each be met, demonstrated and admired, with the domestic story fitted into the gaps between exhibits. The Middletons are billed as an average American family, which in a film built this way is a specification rather than an observation: a household calibrated to want exactly what the fair has on display. Watched now, the interest inverts. The appliances are antiques and the pitch behind them is completely exposed, so what remains is a year explaining to itself, at feature length, how the near future was going to feel.

Everyone doing the talking is old, and the events they describe lie sixty years and more behind them. That gap is the method rather than a limitation. Stewart Bird went looking for surviving members of the Industrial Workers of the World, founded in Chicago in 1905 to organise across trades rather than within them, while there were still people who could describe a strike from inside it. What comes back is talk, and songs the movement carried, and photographs of picket lines whose participants are now sitting in a chair in front of a camera. The archive footage supplies the crowds; the interviews supply what the crowds were for. Eighty-nine minutes, much of it a face and a memory, which by 1979 was the only form this material could take.

A love story in which the decisive institution is a county council. South Riding takes Winifred Holtby's proposition seriously, that local government is the front line against sickness, poverty and ignorance, and spends much of its eighty-five minutes on Yorkshire committee business: what land is bought, whose interest is quietly served, which improvements are funded and which are not. The National Board of Review put it among its ten best of the year. The romance runs through the machinery rather than over it. A squire whose wife is in a mental hospital, and a schoolmistress with plans for other people's children, are both in council terms applicants for something. Victor Saville keeps six officials on screen long enough that their private trouble arrives at the same table as their votes.
